question: Why do we expect a bad event to hurt longer than it actually does?
answer: Gilbert calls it the impact bias: we imagine the event, a break-up, a lost election, a failed exam, and forget everything else that will fill our days. We also forget our 'psychological immune system', which quietly finds silver linings. Most people recover faster than they predicted.
move: Bad news usually hurts less, and for less long, than you fear.
simply: When you picture failing a test, you picture only the test. Real life after it has friends, food and football, which take up most of your attention.
why: Fear of how bad we will feel stops people leaving bad jobs, ending bad relationships or taking good risks. Expecting to recover makes better choices possible.

book.title: Stumbling on Happiness
book.author: Daniel Gilbert
book.badge: Winner of the Royal Society Prize for Science Books

reference: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness (Knopf, 2006), ch. 8
